blueprint.concept: A focused Strange History & True Stories channel built around “Animals That Changed History,” using original research, clear storytelling, and a disciplined Shorts-to-long-form system.
blueprint.promise: True stories from the past that sound fictional—researched, visualized, and explained without turning legend into fact.
blueprint.targetAudience: Curious English-speaking viewers aged 18–44 who like documentary Shorts and surprising evidence-led stories.
blueprint.viewerDesire: Understand something surprising quickly and trust that the creator separated evidence from exaggeration.
pillars: How one event changed what followed
blueprint.visualIdentity: Dark documentary studio, clean direct captions, one focal image per scene, restrained cyan/amber accents, no fake archival labels.
blueprint.languageStrategy: Write natively in English for international viewers. Use concise vocabulary, neutral pronunciation, and English captions. Do not translate Thai scripts literally.
blueprint.shortsStrategy: Publish 3–5 Shorts per week, test three hook families, and create sequels only when at least two performance signals beat the channel median.
blueprint.longFormStrategy: Every 8–10 Shorts, expand the strongest topic into a 6–9 minute evidence-led video to build watch time and authority.

Days 31–60: double down on the strongest series; produce two long-form expansions.

risks: Competition is global; generic AI visuals and translated scripts will underperform.
A single template repeated across the channel may create inauthentic-content risk.
Claims and realistic AI reconstructions require a documented review workflow.
blueprint.originalityStrategy: Keep a research record, write each script from a unique angle, vary scene logic—not only colors or names—and save editing decisions that prove transformation.
factCheckWorkflow: List every factual claim and classify it as documented, reported, disputed, or unsupported.
Verify with at least two credible sources where practical; prefer primary or official records.
Add caveats directly to the narration when evidence is uncertain.
Run a final visual-era, rights, and synthetic-disclosure review before publishing.
blueprint.sourcePolicy: Use primary or official sources first, then reputable secondary analysis. Save URLs, publisher, access date, and the exact claim supported. Never invent a citation.
decisionCriteria: Continue if at least two of 12 Shorts beat the channel median on retention and subscriber conversion.
Pivot the hook or sub-series if views rise but subscribers and returning viewers remain weak.
Stop or park the channel if production cost stays high and no repeatable winner appears after 30 tested videos.

projects.title: Wojtek: The Soldier Bear
projects.researchSummary: Authoritative museum records document Wojtek’s association with Polish soldiers, his wartime journey and later life in Edinburgh. Retellings about ammunition handling need careful wording.
projects.factCheckSummary: Formal enlistment and unit-emblem context are safe. Use “according to accounts” for ammunition-carrying details and label visuals as reconstruction.
projects.hook: This bear was not just a mascot—he was formally enlisted so he could travel with Polish soldiers.
projects.script: This bear was not just a mascot. Wojtek travelled with Polish soldiers during the Second World War. Accounts connect him with the Italian campaign and Monte Cassino, but details about carrying ammunition are told differently across sources. What is documented is that the unit adopted a bear carrying a shell as its emblem. Wojtek survived the war and later lived in Edinburgh Zoo—becoming a symbol of the soldiers who had lost their home but not their identity.
